questions.q: What GPU utilization pattern is the strongest early signal of data-loading starvation rather than a compute or network bottleneck?
options: GPU utilization is consistently at 100% the entire run
GPU utilization dips rhythmically at the start of each step and recovers once the batch arrives
GPU utilization is zero for the entire job
GPU memory usage grows without bound
questions.explain: A recurring stall right when the next batch should load, with otherwise healthy utilization, points specifically at the data loader rather than communication or compute.

questions.q: A node's CPU utilization is pegged near 100% while GPU utilization dips during training. What does this symptom most likely indicate?
options: The GPU is overheating
CPU-bound preprocessing, such as tokenization or decompression, is saturating the node's CPU cores
The network fabric has failed
The checkpoint is corrupted
questions.explain: Expensive per-sample preprocessing can max out CPU cores before any other part of the pipeline becomes the limit, which shows up as high CPU and dipping GPU utilization together.

questions.q: What does the PyTorch Profiler's trace, viewed in TensorBoard, actually show?
options: The model's final accuracy on a held-out test set
A breakdown of each step's time into data-loading wait, compute, and communication segments
The dollar cost of the training run
A visualization of the model's architecture only
questions.explain: The profiler trace breaks step time into concrete segments, turning a vague sense that 'GPUs feel slow' into a specific, actionable measurement.

questions.q: Why does increasing `num_workers` eventually make step time worse instead of better?
options: PyTorch has a hard-coded maximum of 4 workers
Each node has a fixed number of CPU cores, so workers eventually compete for the same resources, increasing context-switching and memory pressure
More workers always reduce GPU memory capacity
Workers above a certain count are silently ignored by the DataLoader
questions.explain: num_workers has a ceiling because workers share a fixed CPU core pool; past that ceiling, overhead from competition grows faster than throughput gains.

questions.q: Both CPU and GPU utilization are low at the same time, with no obvious compute bottleneck. What does this combination most likely point to?
options: A storage throughput limit — time is being spent waiting on I/O rather than CPU or GPU work
The model has finished training
pin_memory is set to True
The batch size is too large
questions.explain: When neither CPU nor GPU is the bottleneck but the step is still slow, the likely explanation is that the pipeline is waiting on storage or network I/O, such as streaming shards directly from S3 without a warm cache.
